headline: A Bent Outrigger, Two Bigeye, and the Long Tow Back from the Break
subhead: The canyon fleet out of Montauk and Block Island found the color again this week, but the run to it is still the whole game.
body_markdown:
The radio traffic Tuesday night told the story before any boat hit the dock. A 38-footer running out of Montauk was calling ahead for a tow — not because anything was wrong with the boat, but because the starboard outrigger had folded on a double header of bigeye somewhere out past the drop, and the mate wanted a heads up that they'd be limping in slow on one working rigger and a lot of stories. Two fish in the box, one that got the leader wrapped around a prop wash and went home with the fish instead of the boat. That's the canyon trade this time of year — you get paid, but you pay something back.

The week itself held up better than a lot of the fleet expected. The warm filament that's been draped across the eastern grounds since late August hasn't slid off or broken down, and the eddy sitting on it has stayed put long enough for boats running from Montauk, Block Island, and the Rhode Island ports to actually plan around it instead of chasing it. That's the difference between a good week and a wasted tank of fuel out here — when the break holds still for four or five days, the fleet stops guessing and starts working it like a spot instead of a moving target.

Water on the temperature edges toward Veatch and Hydrographer has been running cooler than what's sitting over the canyons to the west, but it's still holding bigeye and yellowfin right on the seam where the cooler green water meets the blue. That's not a knock — cooler doesn't mean dead, it means the fish are stacked tighter on the edge instead of spread out, which is actually easier fishing if you find the line and stay on it. Boats that trolled the break itself, working back and forth across the color change instead of running straight through it, did better than the ones that just ran the numbers and hoped.

The standout of the week, though, has been the daytime swordfish drop. Several boats making the extended run out toward Oceanographer have had exceptional results suspending live squid around 200 feet on the daytime drop — not the deep overnight stuff, the shallower daytime presentation with a glow stick and enough lead to hold position in the current. That's a long day and a long run to set up one drop, but the results have been good enough that word is spreading fast in the marina lots. If you've got the fuel and the patience to make that trip worthwhile, this is the week to try it, because a bite like this on the day drop doesn't always last.

On the troll, the spread that's been working is the same one that always works out here when the fish are on bait and not just running the temp break out of habit — green-and-yellow ballyhoo skirts and naked ballyhoo pulled off the riggers, a bird or two well back to keep the spread lively, and a couple of cedar plugs or small tuna feathers in the shotgun position for anything that comes up short. Yellowfin have been running mixed sizes, mostly mid-30s to 50-pound class, with the occasional bigger fish mixed in on the troll and a better shot at real bigeye on the drop-back or the night chunk once the boat commits to anchoring up on the edge. Mahi have been scattered under whatever floating junk the current pushes together — a few boats picked up decent numbers working pot warps and any weed lines they crossed on the way out, so it pays to keep a rod rigged with a small skirted jig even while you're running.

Wahoo have been a bonus fish rather than a target — a couple came aboard on high-speed lures pulled well back in the spread, but nobody's dedicating a whole trip to them yet. White marlin sightings have been light this week, more shots than hookups, which tracks with a canyon system that's still cooler than peak and hasn't fully turned over into the late-summer pattern.

The moon is the thing to watch now. New moon lands September 10, and if the warm filament holds through that window the way it's held the last several days, this sets up as the best stretch the eastern grounds have had all season — tighter tides usually mean better current on the edges, and better current means the bait stacks harder against the break instead of drifting through it. That's when the bigeye bite tends to turn from a night program into an all-day proposition, and it's worth planning a trip around rather than squeezing one in between other commitments.

The catch, and there's always a catch out here, is that this is still the longest run in the region. A boat leaving Montauk or Block Island for Atlantis or Veatch is committing the better part of a tank and a full day before the first bait even hits the water, and the Rhode Island boats running for Oceanographer or Hydrographer aren't getting there any cheaper. If the forecast holds flat through the weekend and the filament doesn't slide off the edge, the window is real. If a front pushes through and stirs the break apart, the fish scatter and the run stops paying for itself. Check the latest before committing fuel — but as of this week, the grounds are worth the trip, and the fleet that's willing to put in the miles has been coming home with fish to show for it.
